lede: Two square numbers with a minus between them factorise on sight: $a^2 - b^2$ is always $(a + b)(a - b)$. It is the one factorisation with no searching in it, and it is also the trick that turns $83^2 - 17^2$ into $100 \times 66$ in your head.
can: Spot a difference of two squares: two terms, both squares, a minus between.
Factorise with the number first, keeping the order the question gives.
Take out a common factor, then look for the pattern again.

md: This is the one factorisation that does not need any searching. Two terms, both squares, a minus between them — and the answer is written down in a single line. Its real value comes later: it is the step that unlocks the hardest algebraic-fraction questions in M4, and it turns $83^2 - 17^2$ into something you can do in your head.

md: Take a square of side $a$ and cut a square of side $b$ out of one corner. What is left has area $a^2 - b^2$. Now cut the remaining L-shape into two rectangles and slide them together:

prompt: A square of side $a$ has a square of side $b$ cut from one corner. What area is left?
explain: The whole square is $a^2$ and the piece removed is $b^2$, so $a^2 - b^2$ is left. The next step slides that same area into one rectangle.

md:
The rectangle is $(a + b)$ long and $(a - b)$ high, so $a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b)$.
The algebra says the same thing: $(a + b)(a - b) = a^2 - ab + ab - b^2$, and the two middle products are equal and opposite, so they cancel. **That is why there is no middle term** — and it is also the check. If you expand your brackets and a middle term survives, the signs are wrong.

In $36 - p^2$ the number comes first, so the **number** leads both brackets: $(6 + p)(6 - p)$.
Turning it round to $(p + 6)(p - 6)$ gives $p^2 - 36$ — the negative of what was asked. The two differ by a factor of $-1$, and a marker will not accept one for the other.

title: Summer 2025 M4 Q20
md: The identity itself was known. It went wrong whenever the letter was not the first term: candidates swapped the terms round and factorised as though the square of the letter came first. Full-mark answers kept the terms in the order given and then cancelled whole brackets.

explain: The second gives $w^2 - 100$; the third has a middle term.

md:
A term is a perfect square when its **coefficient** is a square number and its **index** is even. So:
$4x^2 = (2x)^2$, because $2x \times 2x = 4x^2$.
$25a^2 = (5a)^2$ and $4b^2 = (2b)^2$, so $25a^2 - 4b^2 = (5a + 2b)(5a - 2b)$.
$\dfrac{x^2}{4} = \left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)^2$, so $\dfrac{x^2}{4} - 9 = \left(\dfrac{x}{2} + 3\right)\left(\dfrac{x}{2} - 3\right)$.
The commonest loss is rooting the letter and forgetting the number, which gives brackets that expand to the wrong thing.

text: Common factor first, then look again

md:
$5x^2 - 45$ is **not** a difference of two squares as it stands, because $5x^2$ is not a perfect square. Take the common factor out and it becomes one:
$5x^2 - 45 = 5(x^2 - 9) = 5(x + 3)(x - 3)$.
That is what **'factorise fully'** is asking for. Two half-answers lose marks: stopping at $5(x^2 - 9)$, and hiding the factor inside as $(2n + 6)(2n - 6)$ — which expands correctly but leaves a 2 in each bracket.
The habit worth building: after every common factor, ask the question again. Is what is left still a difference of two squares?

$x^2 + 25$ is a **sum** of two squares. There is no factorisation with real numbers, and rearranging will not produce one. Two terms and a plus sign means stop.
$x^2 - 20$ has only one perfect square: 20 is not a square number, so this needs surds and is not part of this statement.
And 'factorise' never means 'solve'. $(x + 5)(x - 5)$ is a complete answer; adding $= 0$, or offering $x = 5$ and $x = -5$, answers a different question.

explain: A sum of two squares has no real factorisation. The other two are $(x + 6)(x - 6)$ and $(6 + x)(6 - x)$.

title: Why a sum will not factorise
md: Two brackets avoid a middle term only when their middle products cancel, and that needs one plus bracket and one minus bracket. A plus between the two squares leaves nothing to cancel, so there are no brackets to find.

M3 gives you a calculator, but M7 Paper 1 does not, and there the identity is a shortcut worth knowing:
$83^2 - 17^2 = (83 + 17)(83 - 17) = 100 \times 66 = 6600$.
$101^2 - 99^2 = 200 \times 2 = 400$.
Two squares you would not want to work out become one easy product. Watch the trap: $(83 - 17)^2$ is a different number entirely.

The reason this identity is worth more than its two marks is what it does to fractions:
$\dfrac{x^2 - 16}{x + 4} = \dfrac{(x + 4)(x - 4)}{x + 4} = x - 4$.
Nothing cancels until the top is factorised, and only **whole brackets** cancel — crossing out the $x^2$ against the $x$ is worth nothing. That is the M4 question this topic is preparing you for.

Spot two squares with a minus between them.
Keep the order given, so the first term leads both brackets.
Take a common factor out first, then look again.
Use the identity as arithmetic when there is no calculator.

In this unit it is one or two marks, usually one part of a two-part factorise question. The first mark, where there is one, is for showing the pattern: writing $64 = 8^2$ and $9k^2 = (3k)^2$. The last is the pair of brackets in the order given, fully factorised. Stuck: expand your answer back — the middle terms must cancel and the two ends must match the question, signs included.

title: Not on this spec
md: Sums of two squares do not factorise. Differences where a term is not a perfect square ($x^2 - 20$) would need surds, and differences of cubes ($x^3 - 8$) are not on this specification. Solving is M3-NA-11.
